transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. What brings you in to see me today?

I came in because I can’t stop noticing how uneven and puffy the left side of my face looks, especially on video calls and in salsa photos. Everyone tells me they don’t see it, but it’s been getting in the way of work and being social.
On an average day, roughly how many hours would you say you spend thinking about or checking the appearance of your face?

A few hours, probably—especially before meetings or if I’m going out. I keep checking the camera preview, changing the angle or lighting, fixing my hair to cover that side, retaking pictures, and asking friends if I look strange. Sometimes it goes on until I’m late or just too drained to go.
When friends tell you they don't notice any unevenness, how convinced are you that they're wrong versus considering they might be right?

Most of the time I think they’re wrong, or maybe they’re just being nice. I know they say they don’t see it, but when I see myself on the camera or in photos, that left side looks obviously uneven and puffy to me. Part of me wonders if I’m over-focusing on it, but I still can’t really believe it isn’t there.

Aside from your concerns about your face, have you noticed any other unusual thoughts, beliefs, or experiences—like feeling that people are watching you, talking about you, or hearing things others don't hear?
No, I haven’t noticed anything like that. I don’t feel like people are watching or talking about me, and I haven’t heard things other people don’t hear.
Is there ever a moment—even for a few seconds—when you can genuinely consider that the unevenness might just be your perception and not really there, or does it always feel completely certain to you?

I can consider it for a few seconds, especially when everyone says they don’t see it. But then I see myself on a video call or in a salsa photo, and it looks so obvious to me that I go right back to thinking it’s really there.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient demonstrates a persistent, distressing preoccupation with a perceived facial asymmetry/puffiness that is not observable or is only slight to others, accompanied by repetitive checking, camouflaging, and reassurance-seeking behaviors that impair social and occupational functioning. Insight is fair-to-poor (able to briefly consider the belief may be inaccurate but reverts to conviction), without fixed delusional certainty, and no other psychotic symptoms (no ideas of reference, hallucinations, or paranoia) are present, ruling out a primary psychotic disorder such as delusional disorder. The clinical picture is consistent with Body Dysmorphic Disorder (classified under Hypochondriacal Disorder, F45.22, in ICD-10).

Preoccupation occurs especially during video calls and photos

Seeking reassurance from friends about appearance
Able to briefly consider (for a few seconds) that the perceived flaw may not be real when others deny seeing it
Reverts to strong conviction that the flaw is present after seeing self on camera or in photos
Denies ideas of reference or feeling watched/talked about
